prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: World University Rankings 2024: Top Seven (language en).
Grid: 7 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "University" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Country" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Score" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Overall rank" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "University" · longest unbreakable word 109px · one-line width 277px
  col 2: header "Country" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 111px
  col 3: header "Score › Teaching" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 65px
  col 4: header "Score › Research" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 67px
  col 5: header "Score › Citations" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 65px
  col 6: header "Score › Industry" · longest unbreakable word 60px · one-line width 60px
  col 7: header "Overall rank" · longest unbreakable word 51px · one-line width 86px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 729px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 728px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 729px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare the top seven universities by their overall rank and four component scores, with country providing context.","reading":"Readers identify a university, scan across its row for scores and rank, and compare values down each score column. Longer university names can wrap within their own rows; the two-level header gives the spanning headers room to wrap.","groups":["Teaching, Research, Citations and Industry are parallel scores under the shared Score heading and should have comparable widths.","University and Country identify each institution; Overall rank is a separate summary measure."],"keep_intact":["Individual words in university and country names","Score values and rank numbers","Each score subheader"],"may_wrap":["University names at word boundaries","Country names at the space between words","Overall rank header between its two words"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[210,105,86,88,86,81,72],"idea":"Balance room for university names and countries while keeping the four score columns close in width and wrapping the rank header."},{"name":"B","widths":[170,132,86,88,86,81,85],"idea":"Keep country names on one line and give rank more room, accepting additional wrapping in university names."},{"name":"C","widths":[230,82,86,88,86,81,75],"idea":"Favor university names as the main row identifiers, allowing two-word country names and the rank header to wrap."}]}
